happened: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14151, which ended diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, offices and trainings inside federal agencies. A January 29, 2025 order on K-12 schools told agencies to plan to cut federal funds that support teaching certain race-based concepts. Congress has not passed a law banning federal funding of critical race theory training.

key_dates.event: Executive Order 14151 ends federal DEI programs and trainings.
Order on K-12 schooling targets federal funding tied to certain race-based teaching.

legal: A federal court in Maryland preliminarily blocked parts of Executive Orders 14151 and 14173 in February 2025 (NADOHE v. Trump); the Fourth Circuit paused that order in March 2025 and vacated it on February 6, 2026, finding the orders likely not unconstitutional on their face. The case continues in the district court. The end of DEI trainings inside federal agencies was not blocked.
closeness: Same goal, partly the same mechanism. The orders use the terms DEI and "discriminatory equity ideology" rather than "critical race theory," and no law was passed.
uncertain: A new request for a preliminary injunction in NADOHE was filed in June 2026; I did not find a ruling on it. I found no bill on critical race theory funding among the laws passed by the 119th Congress. Newest source is from February 2026.

happened: Executive Order 14173 (January 21, 2025) told the Attorney General and agency heads to enforce civil rights laws against private-sector DEI practices that use racial preferences. In 2026 the EEOC acted on this: on February 26 its chair warned the 500 largest U.S. companies about Title VII liability for race- and sex-based DEI programs, and in March it announced a $500,000 settlement over an employer's DEI practices. On March 26, 2026, Executive Order 14398 required a contract clause barring federal contractors from "racially discriminatory DEI activities."

legal: The Fourth Circuit on February 6, 2026 vacated a preliminary injunction against parts of Executive Order 14173 (NADOHE v. Trump), so enforcement continues while the case goes on. No court ruling on Executive Order 14398 was found.
closeness: Same goal. The EEOC is now using Title VII against DEI programs, as recommended, but the President's direction came through general orders rather than a specific directive about critical race theory trainings.
uncertain: How many Title VII lawsuits (not just letters, subpoenas and settlements) the EEOC and DOJ have filed over DEI. Newest source is from mid-2026.

happened: Congress has not changed Title VII or other laws to end disparate impact claims. On April 23, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14281, which told agencies to stop prioritizing disparate impact cases, including under Title VII. The Justice Department removed disparate impact from its Title VI rules in December 2025, and Commerce, DHS, Transportation, HHS and Education did the same in 2026.

happened: NLRB General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo left in late January 2025 after President Trump took office, and on February 3, 2025 he named William Cowen acting general counsel. EEOC General Counsel Karla Gilbride was removed on January 27, 2025, and the President named Andrew Rogers acting EEOC general counsel. Crystal Carey became NLRB general counsel in January 2026. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Trump v. Slaughter that the FTC's for-cause removal protection is unconstitutional.

key_dates.event: EEOC General Counsel Gilbride removed.
Trump appoints William Cowen acting NLRB general counsel.
Crystal Carey takes office as NLRB general counsel.
Supreme Court decides Trump v. Slaughter on removal protections.

legal: In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held the FTC Act's for-cause removal provision violates the separation of powers, supporting the President's power to remove officials with fixed terms.
closeness: Direct match: both the NLRB and EEOC general counsels were replaced in the first two weeks.
uncertain: How the Slaughter ruling applies to NLRB and EEOC members specifically. Newest source is June 2026.

happened: On January 20, 2025, President Trump froze federal civilian hiring across the executive branch, including the Labor Department. The freeze was replaced on October 15, 2025 by Executive Order 14356, which says no vacant job may be filled unless a new Strategic Hiring Committee in each agency approves it.

key_dates.event: Presidential memorandum freezes federal civilian hiring.
Executive Order 14356 replaces the freeze with committee approval for each hire.

legal: No court ruling blocking the freeze or Executive Order 14356 was found.
closeness: Broader in scope (all agencies, not just labor agencies). The flat freeze ended, but hiring still needs special approval.
uncertain: How many career hires the labor agencies made in 2025-2026. Newest source is October 2025.
